source_refs.note: Exercise 10.1, Question 4: book page 278 (Q1-Q24). The book prints no answers for Exercise 10.1.

blocks.explanation:
An equation in \(\csc^{2}x\): isolate it, change to \(\sin^{2}x\), take the square root with \(\pm\).
We get \(\sin x = \pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), two basic equations.
Plan: solve both in \([0, 2\pi]\), check that \(\csc x\) is defined, then add \(2\pi\).
steps:
Given: \(9 - 3\csc^{2}x = 5\).
To find: principal solutions and general solution.
Method: isolate \(\csc^{2}x\), use \(\sin x = \frac{1}{\csc x}\), take the square root, solve two basic sine equations.

Isolate \(\csc^{2}x\)
\[3\csc^{2}x = 9 - 5 = 4\]
\[\csc^{2}x = \dfrac{4}{3}\]
Why: move \(3\csc^{2}x\) to the right and 5 to the left, then divide by 3.

Change to sine
\[\sin^{2}x = \dfrac{3}{4}\]
\[\sin x = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
Why: \(\sin x = \frac{1}{\csc x}\), so \(\sin^{2}x\) is the reciprocal of \(\frac{4}{3}\); the square root has two signs.

When \(\sin x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) (quadrants I, II)
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
\[x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\]
Why: sine is positive in quadrants I and II.

When \(\sin x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) (quadrants III, IV)
\[x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\]
\[x = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\]
Why: sine is negative in quadrants III and IV.

Is \(\csc x\) defined?
None of these angles makes \(\sin x = 0\), so \(\csc x\) exists at all four and all four are valid.
Why: \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\) is undefined only where \(\sin x = 0\).

General solution
The period of \(\sin x\) is \(2\pi\):
\[\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\]
\[\cup \left\{\dfrac{2\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\]
\[\cup \left\{\dfrac{4\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\]
\[\cup \left\{\dfrac{5\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Why: each principal solution generates its own family.

Check
At each of the four angles \(\sin^{2}x = \frac{3}{4}\), so
\[\csc^{2}x = \dfrac{4}{3}\]
\[9 - 3 \cdot \dfrac{4}{3} = 9 - 4 = 5\]
Why: the left side equals the right side.
blocks.final_answer: Principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}\). General solution: \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\) \(\cup\) \(\left\{\frac{2\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\) \(\cup\) \(\left\{\frac{4\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\) \(\cup\) \(\left\{\frac{5\pi}{3} + 2n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\). (Shorter form: \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\), since \(\frac{4\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3} + \pi\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \pi\).)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 10.1. Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. As in the book's examples, we give the principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\) and the general solution as a union of sets.
